Utterance: Asking children about potential traumas is essential as adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) significantly impact lifelong health. Dr. Lawson previously assessed 10-year-old Sam's ACE score as three based on his mother's report. Now, she interviews Sam alone to confirm these findings.
Hi Sam, thanks for waiting. I talked to your mom about things at home and school. Now I'm going to ask you some screening questions I ask all kids. Feel free to ask me anything as we talk, okay?
Okay, I guess.
First, how have things been going at home?
Okay, I guess.
How's your mom doing? Is there ever a time where she isn't able to get out of bed or do what she needs to do?
No, she's looking after me most of the time.
What does most of the time mean? Is there anything she could do better?
Maybe getting dinner, because sometimes I just have to get a bowl of Cheerios for myself.
How many times a week are you having Cheerios for dinner? Is your mom with you?
Pretty much every day, and I'm mainly by myself.
Is there enough food in the fridge? Have you been worried about it, or about having a winter coat and boots?
No. My mom says we'll go shopping, but we never do because she's too busy.
Are there times your mom seems down or upset for days at a time?
She might be a little stressed because of Grandma. They've been arguing and yelling a lot.
Tell me more about that. Have you ever been afraid someone might get hurt?
They argue about things. I just go to my room. Once, maybe, I was afraid because they were getting really mean.
How intense does it get? Has anybody been physical, used fists, or thrown objects? Where are you during this?
No, I just go to my room and try to ignore it. Afterwards, they just stay away from each other for a while.
Has anyone ever said mean or hurtful things to you?
Sometimes my grandma criticizes me and won't help me with what I'm doing wrong.
What about your mom? Also, has anyone ever touched your body in an inappropriate or sexual way?
Not that I know. And no to the other thing.
Does anyone hit or spank you, or hurt your body physically?
No.
Is there any drug or alcohol use in your home that worries you?
No.
How do you feel in your close relationships? Do you feel loved and cared about?
My mom pays more attention to my little brother. When I want something, she doesn't really listen and won't really ask me later.
Is there any adult you feel loved by or would go to for help?
I like to be in my room. I wouldn't have anybody. I just go to my room and think.
Has anyone been in jail? What are the main stressors at home?
No. The stressors are the fighting with Grandma and my dad moving away because they got divorced.
Do you see your dad? When was the last time?
No, not since a year ago. There's no plan to see him.
I hear that there are stressors like the arguing, your dad moving away, and not always feeling loved. Do you think that makes school hard?
I think so. I'm thinking about that instead of what I'm doing, so I don't get a lot done.
That makes sense. When things are stressful at home, kids have trouble concentrating. I'll talk to your mom and figure out how to help you both. Thanks for coming in.

Sam's interview confirms his ACE score is three due to parental loss, physical neglect, and emotional deprivation. Dr. Lawson can now collaboratively develop an evidence-based intervention plan to help change Sam's lifetime health trajectory.
